title: Assigning Clear Ownership Using the RACI Matrix

sources.title: A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide)
sources.reference: Project Management Institute. A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide).
sources.note: PMBOK identifies RACI as a standard example of a Responsibility Assignment Matrix. RACI has no single founding author and descends from mid-20th-century linear responsibility chart practice; this RLO therefore presents it as a stable practitioner convention rather than attributing it to a founding paper.

terminal_objective: Given a list of project tasks and stakeholders, assign RACI roles correctly for each task, with exactly one Accountable and at least one Responsible per task.
performance_context: Use a RACI matrix before or during cross-functional project and operational work to clarify who performs work, owns outcomes, contributes input, and receives updates.

enabling_objective.statement: Assign Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed roles to a task while applying the structural rules of a valid RACI matrix.

concepts.name: Responsible
concepts.definition: The person or people who do the work required to complete the task.
concepts.elaboration: Responsible describes execution, not ultimate ownership. Ask who is actually performing the work. A task must have at least one Responsible person or role.

misconceptions.statement: Responsible and Accountable are interchangeable labels for the person most involved in a task.
misconceptions.correction: Responsible performs the work; Accountable is the one person who ultimately answers for the outcome. One person may hold both roles, but the roles describe different responsibilities.

concepts.name: Accountable
concepts.definition: The single person who ultimately answers for whether the task is completed correctly.
concepts.elaboration: Every task row has exactly one Accountable person or role, even when several people are Responsible. Ask whose name is called if the outcome is not delivered correctly.

misconceptions.statement: Assigning multiple Accountable people creates shared ownership and reduces risk.
misconceptions.correction: Multiple Accountable assignments diffuse ownership and recreate the ambiguity RACI is intended to remove. Select exactly one Accountable per task.

misconceptions.statement: A task can omit Accountable when the team shares responsibility informally.
misconceptions.correction: A valid RACI row names exactly one Accountable owner; shared informal ownership does not establish who ultimately answers for the result.

concepts.name: Consulted
concepts.definition: People whose input is actively sought before or during the work through two-way communication.
concepts.elaboration: Consulted roles contribute expertise, requirements, or review that can influence the work before it moves forward.

misconceptions.statement: Anyone who should know about a task should be marked Consulted.
misconceptions.correction: Consulted requires two-way dialogue that can influence the work. A person who only needs a status or outcome notification is Informed.

concepts.name: Informed
concepts.definition: People who receive one-way updates on progress or outcome without needing to weigh in first.
concepts.elaboration: Informed roles need awareness, not participation in the decision or work. Distinguishing them from Consulted roles prevents unnecessary review cycles.

misconceptions.statement: Marking more stakeholders Consulted is always safer than marking them Informed.
misconceptions.correction: Unnecessary consultation can slow decisions. Use Consulted only when two-way input is needed; otherwise use Informed.

concepts.name: RACI matrix structural rules
concepts.definition: A valid RACI matrix uses tasks or decisions as rows, people or roles as columns, and R, A, C, I, or blank as cell values; each row has exactly one A and at least one R.
concepts.elaboration: A row may have zero or more Consulted and Informed assignments. The same person may hold R and A on a small team, but that combination should be deliberate. The one-Accountable and at-least-one-Responsible rules can be validated mechanically.

canonical_content.situation: A task stalls because several people believed someone else owned the decision, while stakeholders expected to be consulted only hear about it after completion.
canonical_content.purpose: A RACI matrix makes execution, outcome ownership, input, and notification explicit before ambiguity delays the work.

responsible.diagnostic_question: Who is actually sitting down and doing this?

accountable.diagnostic_question: If this goes wrong, whose name gets called, and is it exactly one person?

consulted.diagnostic_question: Whose expertise must influence the work before it moves forward?

informed.diagnostic_question: Who needs a heads-up without needing to weigh in first?

canonical_content.shape: Matrix with tasks or decisions as rows and people or roles as columns.
canonical_content.allowed_cell_values: R, A, C, I, or blank.

rules.accountable: Exactly one A per row: never zero and never more than one.
rules.responsible: At least one R per row so someone performs the work.
rules.consulted_informed: C requires two-way dialogue; I requires only one-way communication.
rules.combined_role: The same person may hold R and A when intentional, particularly on small teams.

canonical_content.reasoning: The analyst drafts the report, the department head owns the final result, Legal contributes input before publication, and adjacent teams receive the completed update. The row has exactly one A and at least one R.

canonical_content.violation: The row has two Accountable assignments.
canonical_content.correction: Choose the one person who ultimately answers for approval. If the other person's input is required, assign that person C rather than a second A.

canonical_content.prompt: Review one task row. Confirm exactly one A and at least one R, then ask whether each C truly needs two-way input and each I needs only an update.
validation_order: Test I assignments for notification only

assessment_items.stem: A RACI row assigns the Project Sponsor and Department Head as Accountable for the same task. What is the primary problem?

options.text: The row diffuses outcome ownership by assigning more than one Accountable.
options.feedback: Correct. Each task must have exactly one Accountable owner.

options.text: Every task must use a different person for Responsible and Accountable.
options.feedback: R and A describe different roles, but one person may intentionally hold both. The violation here is two A assignments.

options.text: The row needs an additional Accountable as a tie-breaker.
options.feedback: Adding another A increases ambiguity. Select exactly one person who ultimately owns the outcome.

options.text: There is no problem because accountability should always be shared.
options.feedback: RACI uses exactly one A per row specifically to avoid diffuse accountability.

assessment_items.stem: Legal must review a proposed public statement and provide changes before release. Which RACI role best fits Legal?

options.feedback: Legal is not described as producing the statement; its required contribution is input before release.
The scenario does not make Legal the single owner of the statement's outcome.
Correct. Legal provides two-way input that can change the work before it proceeds.
Informed is one-way communication. Required review and changes make Legal Consulted.

assessment_items.stem: Which assignment is structurally valid for one task row?

options.text: Two A assignments, one R assignment, and one I assignment
options.feedback: The row has more than one Accountable owner.

options.text: One A assignment, zero R assignments, and two C assignments
options.feedback: The row needs at least one Responsible person to perform the work.

options.text: One A assignment, two R assignments, one C assignment, and one I assignment
options.feedback: Correct. The row has exactly one A and at least one R; multiple R assignments and optional C and I assignments are allowed.

options.text: Zero A assignments, one R assignment, and one C assignment
options.feedback: The row needs exactly one Accountable owner.

content.task: Approve a new product launch for compliance review
Approve a change to a production-line safety procedure

design_brief.tone: Practical, direct, and precise corporate training. Emphasize decisions teams must make rather than abstract organizational theory.
design_brief.scaffolding_notes: Assume no prior knowledge of RACI. Teach the R-versus-A and C-versus-I distinctions before asking learners to validate or complete a row.
design_brief.feedback_policy: Name the violated rule or confused role, point to the relevant assignment, and state the correction. Do not place correctness explanations in visible answer-option text; reveal them after submission.
example_shape_hints: Render assignments as a matrix with tasks as rows and stakeholder roles as columns, not as a substitute bulleted list.
Show exactly one A visually and explicitly validate at least one R.
Select a matching approved industry variant when available; definitions and structural rules must not change with context.
practice_shape_hints: Present one row at a time and ask learners to identify a structural or role-assignment error.
Use distractors that target multiple A assignments, missing R assignments, R-versus-A confusion, and C-versus-I confusion.
A format may provide a matrix-building practice interaction, but scored assessment must use approved objective items until constructed-response matrix scoring is supported downstream.
design_brief.salience_hook_description: Establish that unclear ownership causes stalled decisions, duplicated work, and surprise accountability; RACI makes those expectations explicit before work starts.

gagne_event_mapping.event_3_stimulate_recall: Ask the learner to recall a task where ownership or required input was unclear.
gagne_event_mapping.event_7_provide_feedback: Use the per-option feedback in each assessment item and the design brief feedback policy.
gagne_event_mapping.event_9_enhance_retention: Invite the learner to validate one current project task using the one-A, at-least-one-R, C-versus-I checks.

content_type_recommendations.rationale: A matrix interaction can make assignments visible and validate the one-A and at-least-one-R rules immediately.
A visual walkthrough can build and correct a matrix row while highlighting common role confusions.
A project-kickoff conversation can illustrate how a team decides between R and A or C and I for one manageable task.
A blank grid with the four diagnostic questions supports immediate use during project planning.

authoring_rationale: This RLO treats RACI assignment as one integrated procedure because learners must apply the four role definitions and structural constraints together to produce a valid task row. The one-Accountable rule is the central mechanically testable constraint. Definitions, rules, and assessment logic remain constant across contexts; only tasks and stakeholder roles vary.

governance.change_history: v1.0.0 initial RACI matrix sample authored in the unified RLO schema (2026-07-30).

rights.sharing_constraints: Internal only; not for external distribution.
